---
title: "Design Notes"
---

Background on why `daily-dose` is shaped the way it is. For instructions, see the
[Tutorials](../tutorials/index.qmd) or [How-to Guides](../how-to/index.qmd); for exact
signatures, see [Reference](../reference/index.qmd).

## Why just two features

The original site was a full R Markdown site: a page per year, a Notes page, a Dev
page. Converting it kept exactly the two things that make a personal workout log worth
opening day to day — a random pick, and "what did I do on this day before" — rather
than rebuilding a year-by-year browser nobody was asking for. Notes (training
principles) and Dev (untested workout drafts, never real dated entries) were dropped
for the same reason: neither is a *workout*, so neither belongs in a random pick or an
on-this-day match.

## Why one record shape for two very different sources

Roughly 4 years of the history is typed markdown; a stretch of 2020 is photos of a
whiteboard. Rather than model these as two separate collections, every workout is one
record with a `date`, a `kind` (`"text"` or `"image"`), and whichever fields apply to
that kind. This lets both features — `random_workout()` and `on_this_day()` — operate
on a single flat list without caring what's inside each record; only the rendering
layer (`workout_card()`) branches on `kind`.

## Why text wins when a date has both

Some 2020 dates turned out to have *both* a photographed whiteboard and a later typed
write-up of the same session — the photo was a same-day backup, typed up afterward.
Keeping both would mean the same real workout showing up twice under "On This Day," and
"Random Workout" silently double-weighting those dates. The build script resolves this
by preferring the text entry, which also happens to be the richer of the two (it
usually includes rep/set structure the photo doesn't make searchable).

## Why the photos are recompressed

The original whiteboard photos were uncompressed phone-camera PNGs, some over 10MB
each — 325MB total for 120 images. `daily-dose` is a package meant to be installed, not
just a static site, so shipping that weight in every install wasn't worth it. Downscale
and re-encode as JPEG dropped it to ~21MB with no visible loss for what's essentially a
photo of handwriting on a whiteboard.

## Why Shiny Core, not Express

The app is one server function wiring two buttons to two pure functions and a render
call — small enough that Express's terser syntax would save a few lines. It's still
built with Shiny Core: `core.py` has no dependency on Shiny at all, which is what makes
`random_workout()` and `on_this_day()` unit-testable without spinning up a Shiny
session (see `tests/test_core.py`). That separation is the reason `app.py` reads as
thin glue rather than where the logic actually lives.

## Why the parser keeps things it can't fully understand

Four years of hand-typed markdown across five files don't use one consistent format
for exercises, reps, or footnotes. Rather than force that into structured fields and
risk silently mangling entries the parser can't parse confidently, `body_md` keeps the
original markdown for each text entry verbatim, rendered as-is in the app. The only
fields pulled out are the ones that are consistent enough to parse reliably: the date,
the done-checkbox, and an optional video link.
